milestones.label: Voting in federal elections
whatChanges: Citizens meeting the federal age rule can register and cast a ballot, and neither the federal government nor a state may deny the vote on account of age.
Registration deadlines, identification rules, and mail ballot procedures continue to be set state by state, so the practical steps differ across the country.
Not voting remains an ordinary path; many citizens never register, and many register and vote only in some years.

milestones.label: Qualifying for federal jury service
milestones.population: United States citizens residing in a federal judicial district
whatChanges: A person becomes legally qualified to sit on a federal jury, alongside conditions on citizenship, residence in the district, and English proficiency.
Qualifying is not the same as serving; whether a summons ever arrives depends on the district's source lists and random selection.
Many qualified people are never called, and many who are called are excused or not seated.

milestones.label: Selective Service registration requirement
milestones.population: male United States citizens and male immigrants, as the agency records sex for registration
whatChanges: Registration with the Selective Service System becomes a legal requirement for almost everyone in the covered group, and the requirement window closes after the upper age.
The requirement is to register, not to serve; registration by itself does not place anyone in the armed forces.
The rule as written covers men only, so it does not apply to a large share of the population at these ages.

milestones.label: Eligibility to serve in the House of Representatives
milestones.population: United States citizens seeking federal office
whatChanges: Constitutional eligibility for a seat in the House opens, alongside requirements on years of citizenship and inhabiting the represented state.
Eligibility is a floor, not a plan; the overwhelming majority of citizens never seek or hold federal office.

milestones.label: Eligibility to serve in the Senate
milestones.population: United States citizens seeking federal office
whatChanges: Constitutional eligibility for a Senate seat opens, alongside requirements on years of citizenship and residency in the represented state.
The Constitution sets a higher age floor for a seat in the Senate than for a seat in the House, and both floors remain in force.

milestones.label: Eligibility to serve as President
milestones.population: natural born citizens of the United States
whatChanges: Constitutional eligibility for the presidency opens, alongside requirements on being a natural born citizen and years of residence in the country.
This is the highest age floor written into the Constitution for any federal office.

milestones.label: Passport validity period lengthens
whatChanges: A passport issued from this age onward carries the longer adult validity period rather than the shorter one used for younger children.
The length is fixed by age at issuance, so a book issued earlier keeps its shorter term until it expires.
Many people never hold a passport at all, and the change matters only when an application is actually made.
